analysis.one_liner: Doubles oil spill liability limits and forces riskier single-hull tankers to pay more for spills or leave the fleet.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 8, 2004, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: When a tanker spills oil, current law caps how much the company responsible has to pay; after that cap, cleanup costs and damages fall on others, including coastal communities and federal funds. This bill would roughly double those caps, and would phase out caps entirely for older single-hull tankers over six years, while also requiring annual inspections of single-hull tankers older than 15 years and letting port communities ask the Coast Guard to bar tankers that pose a severe risk. It was introduced in the last month of the 108th Congress and died in committee without ever being considered.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near coasts and ports — fishing crews, tourism businesses, waterfront homeowners — gain because spill damage is more likely to be paid by the companies that caused it rather than absorbed by communities, taxpayers, or un-compensated victims. Taxpayers also gain because stronger liability reduces the odds that the public's Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund and federal budgets absorb costs above the caps. Safer double-hull tankers gain a competitive edge over cheaper single-hull rivals.

how_it_helps.text: It doubles the maximum amount polluters must pay for oil spills — for example, the per-ton limit for tank vessels goes from $1,200 to $2,400, and the offshore-facility cap from $75 million to $150 million — so more of the damage from a spill lands on the companies that caused it.
It phases out liability caps for single-hull tank vessels over six years, ending in unlimited liability, which pressures the industry to retire these higher-risk ships rather than keep running them.
It expands who counts as a 'responsible party' so that companies that arrange to ship their oil on an aging single-hull tanker can no longer escape spill costs by pointing at the shipowner.

It requires single-hull tank vessels older than 15 years to pass an annual inspection, and lets port communities ask the Coast Guard to restrict tank vessels that pose a severe risk to their environment, economy, or safety.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker owners, oil companies, and their insurers would bear higher insurance and liability costs, and some of that would likely flow through to fuel prices. Operators of older single-hull vessels would face the steepest squeeze: rising liability each year until 2010, plus annual inspections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil shippers, tanker owners, and insurers

drawbacks.text: Doubling liability limits and phasing in unlimited liability for single-hull vessels would raise the cost of insurance and operation for oil shippers, costs that could be passed partly to consumers through fuel and shipping prices.

The bill would make companies that merely arrange oil shipments on single-hull vessels legally responsible for spills, which industry could fairly argue reaches parties that do not control the ship's condition or operation.

Port-entry restrictions would be set up through regulations requested by port owners, a mechanism that depends entirely on the Coast Guard writing the rules, and the bill gives no penalty if the agency fails to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: when an oil tanker spills, the people and businesses harmed would be paid by the companies responsible rather than left to federal funds or their own lawsuits, and the higher caps and expanded definition of responsible parties would push the industry toward safer double-hull ships. The honest cost is that higher liability means higher insurance and shipping costs for oil transport, some fraction of which could show up in fuel prices, and the open-ended liability for single-hull vessels could hasten their exit from the fleet. Weighed against the cost of a single major spill, which can run into the billions and fall on people who had no say in how the oil was shipped, the tradeoff favors the bill; its serious flaw is timing — it arrived in the final month of a Congress, giving it no realistic chance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final month, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on December 8, 2004, with Sen. Jon Corzine as cosponsor; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward; the Congress ended three and a half weeks later, on January 3, 2005.
The bill never listed more than one cosponsor, so it carried no visible floor support when it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil tanker owners and the companies that ship oil are better off, because spill liability limits stayed at their 1990 levels and single-hull tankers kept capped exposure. Coastal communities and taxpayers remain the ones standing behind spill costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil tanker owners and oil shippers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; both sponsors were New Jersey Democrats, and the committee it was sent to never acted.

industries.note: The bill doubles spill liability limits, phases out liability caps for single-hull vessels over six years, and requires annual inspections of single-hull ships older than 15 years, all of which raise the cost of operating older tankers. This is the industry whose cost of doing business the bill raises.

industries.industry: Oil companies and oil cargo owners
industries.note: The bill redefines 'responsible party' so that companies that arrange oil shipments on single-hull tankers are liable for spills, not just the shipowner. This closes a gap that let oil companies hedge spill risk onto small shipping firms.

Higher liability limits mean larger potential payouts for spill policies, raising premiums and exposure for the insurers who underwrite oil shipments. The cost ultimately flows into the price of shipping oil.

industries.industry: Coastal communities, fisheries, and tourism businesses
industries.note: Stronger liability and inspection rules reduce the chance that a spill's cleanup and economic damage falls on local economies and taxpayers instead of the shippers. These groups bear spill costs today when responsible parties reach their caps.
